kurz: How to make payments from different years comparable, and why the discount rate rests on a judgement.

bloecke.md:
Every sum of money belongs to a point in time. €10,000 today and €10,000 in twenty years are different quantities. This is partly due to rising prices, and partly because money that is available today can be invested until then and earn a return. That is not possible with money that is only paid later. The present value converts any future payment into the amount you would need today to generate it. This makes it possible to compare offers that do not look comparable at first glance, such as a lump sum and instalments, a capital sum and a lifelong pension, or an immediate severance payment and payments continuing over several years.

Discounting means calculating [[compound interest]] backwards. Going forwards, you multiply by (1 + i)^n; going backwards, you divide by the same factor.

bloecke.erklaerung: The factor 1 / (1 + i)^n is called the discount factor. It is less than 1 as long as i is positive.

bloecke.md: At 3.5% (roughly the yield on ten-year German federal bonds in mid-September 2026), a payment of €10,000 in twenty years is worth €5,026 today; at 7%, it is worth only €2,584. The curve falls exponentially. Each additional year of waiting costs the same percentage, but less and less in euros, because the base has already become smaller. This is why payments far in the future hardly carry any weight. For the same reason, you should read with suspicion any calculation whose result comes mainly from the last third of the period.

bloecke.titel: Present value of €10,000 by payment date
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation for the same amount at three discount rates. After thirty years, the difference in value between 2% and 7% is more than €4,000.

bloecke.md:
## Choosing the discount rate

The formula is simple; choosing the interest rate `i` is not. It is made up of three components: the price of the pure shift in time, compensation for the expected loss in the value of money, and a premium for the uncertainty of the payment. For a payment that is practically certain, the interest rate on safe government bonds is a suitable guide. If a payment depends on the continued existence of an employer, a tenant or a business model, a risk premium is added. It belongs either in the discount rate or in the payment itself, but not in both.

If the same stream of payments is discounted at 3% instead of 5%, the result is markedly different. A present value calculation therefore never shows the value of a payment as such. It only shows what the payment would be worth if the best alternative yields x%.

bloecke.md: The discount rate is a statement about the **best alternative** that you give up by waiting for this payment. It is not a property of the payment itself. If the rate cannot be justified, the result is meaningless as a valuation.

## Opportunity cost

[[Opportunity cost]] is the forgone return of the best option not chosen. It never leaves your account and appears on no account statement. That is why it is systematically underestimated, while even a fee of five euros causes annoyance.

A simple example is €20,000 sitting in a current account for five years without interest. Compared with an instant-access savings account at the level of the ECB deposit facility rate of 2.5%, €2,628 is forgone; compared with a safe bond yield of 3.5%, €3,754. None of these amounts is perceived as an expense. Part of it is liquidity paid for deliberately, because an emergency fund is meant to be available and does not need to earn a return. It only becomes a problem when nobody knows what this availability costs.

The same consideration applies wherever capital is tied up without anyone sending an invoice: the paid-off flat that “costs nothing”, the member's share in a cooperative, the rental deposit, the fixed-term deposit with a long lock-in and the interest-free loan to relatives. In all these cases it is not enough to ask what the thing costs. What needs to be checked is what the same money would have earned elsewhere at comparable risk.

bloecke.formel: Present value of perpetuity = C / i        with growth: C / (i − g)
bloecke.erklaerung: An infinite series of discounted payments nevertheless has a finite sum, because the discount factors shrink faster than the payments grow. This requires i to be greater than g.
variablen: Payment per year, first paid in one year

bloecke.md: A pension of €1,000 a month amounts to €12,000 a year. As a perpetuity, it has a present value of €400,000 at a 3% discount rate, but only €200,000 at 6%. The same stream of payments is therefore worth only half as much at double the discount rate. The formula thus delivers two results at once. It shows an upper limit, because no term, however long, can be worth more than the perpetuity. Reversed, it gives the payout rate. €12,000 out of €400,000 corresponds to 3%. To judge whether a pension offer is generous, you therefore first divide the annual payment by the capital and compare the result with the level of interest rates.

With a growing perpetuity, the difference i − g is in the denominator. With i = 3.5% and g = 2.0%, it is 1.5 percentage points. If g is estimated at 2.5%, the denominator falls to 1.0 percentage points, and the present value rises by 50%, even though nothing has changed in reality. Valuations whose result comes mainly from such a terminal value are therefore based on assumptions, even when they are stated to several decimal places.

bloecke.titel: Present value of a pension of €1,000 a month, in thousands of euros
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with annual payments in arrears. The term increases horizontally and the discount rate vertically; in both directions the change in present value becomes smaller with each further step.

bloecke.md:
## Lump sum or pension

Private individuals most often need a present value calculation when they have a choice, for example with a company pension or direct insurance (Direktversicherung) with a lump-sum option, with a severance payment instead of ongoing payments, or with an immediate annuity instead of a lump sum. The comparison is simpler than it looks.

A model case is a contract that offers either €100,000 immediately or €400 a month for life, that is, €4,800 a year. Without interest, the pension would have caught up with the lump sum after 20.8 years. At a discount rate of 2% it takes 27 years, at 3.5% 38 years. If the discount rate is above 4.8%, the ratio of 4,800 to 100,000, the pension never catches up with the lump sum. Even a pension paid forever would then have a lower present value.

bloecke.titel: Present value of €400 a month over 25 years
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation. The line marks the alternative lump sum of €100,000; from a discount rate of about 1.5%, the lump sum is worth more than the pension.

bloecke.md: However, the calculation alone does not settle the question. The lifelong pension is at the same time insurance against a risk that no portfolio covers, namely living for a very long time. A pensioner who is still paying rent at 94 gains nothing from a lump sum that was superior on paper if the account was already empty at 88. On the other hand, insurers calculate the conversion of capital into a pension using deliberately cautious mortality tables. The decisive figure for the comparison is the guaranteed annuity conversion factor (Rentenfaktor), that is, the monthly pension per €10,000 of capital, which is rarely mentioned in advisory meetings. The present value makes it possible to determine the price of this insurance. If the present value of the pension is well below the lump-sum offer, you are paying a high premium for protection against longevity. Whether this premium is worthwhile depends on your personal circumstances and cannot be decided with the formula.

Offer A consists of €60,000 immediately, offer B of five annual instalments of €13,000 each, €65,000 in total. At first glance B looks €5,000 better.

- at a 2.0% discount rate, B is worth €61,275 today and is therefore just ahead
- at 2.73%, the two offers are equivalent
- at 3.5%, B is worth only €58,696, so A is better

The break-even point is therefore below the yield that a safe bond offers in 2026. The calculation also takes into account neither taxes nor the question of whether the payer will still be solvent in five years. Default risk shifts the result further in favour of A. Tax, on the other hand, can also shift it in favour of B. If the interest on the alternative is subject to flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer), around 2.6% of the 3.5% remains, and B is just ahead.

- Calculate with three discount rates instead of one: pessimistic, plausible and optimistic. The result is a range.
- Discount nominal payments at a nominal rate and real payments at a real rate. A company pension without indexation is nominal. Discounting it at a real interest rate ignores the loss of purchasing power entirely and overestimates its present value.
- First determine the payments after tax, then discount them. The reverse order leads to wrong results.
- Write down the discount rate and justify it before calculating. If it is only chosen afterwards, any desired result can be produced.

The tool above values an entire company but uses only the two formulas from this lesson, that is, discounted payments and a growing perpetuity as the terminal value. With the slider for the cost of capital, you can see within a few seconds that a difference of two percentage points in the discount rate can halve the value.

bloecke.titel: Net present value, internal rate of return, calculation accuracy
bloecke.md:
Subtracting the present value of all outflows from the present value of all inflows gives the **net present value** (NPV). If it is positive, the project is worthwhile at the discount rate used. Conversely, if you look for the rate at which the net present value becomes zero, you get the **internal rate of return**, that is, the return of the payment stream. This calculation was carried out twice above, giving 2.73% for the severance payment and 4.8% for the perpetuity.

All calculations in this lesson assume annual payments in arrears. With monthly payments, the money arrives half a year earlier on average, and the present value is 1% to 2% higher, depending on the level of interest rates. For offers that differ by 10%, this makes no difference to the decision, but in close cases it does.

mitnehmen: Future payments only become comparable through discounting, using the formula present value = Z / (1 + i)^n.
The discount rate corresponds to the return on the best alternative forgone, so every valuation is a statement about the available alternatives.
The present value of a perpetuity is the annual payment divided by the interest rate; conversely, the annual payment divided by the capital shows how generous a pension offer is.
Opportunity cost appears on no statement, but is often the largest item in a decision.
When choosing between a lump sum and a pension, the present value provides only part of the answer; the other part is the value of insurance against a very long life.

begriffe.text: The value today of a future payment. It is obtained by dividing the payment by (1 + discount rate) to the power of the number of years.
Interest rate used to discount future payments. It corresponds to the return on the best alternative forgone, including a risk premium.
Stream of payments with no end date. The present value is annual payment / discount rate, or, for a growing payment, annual payment / (discount rate − growth).
Forgone return of the best alternative not chosen. It appears on no statement and is often the largest item when capital is tied up.
Present value of all inflows minus present value of all outflows. If it is positive, the project is worthwhile at the chosen discount rate.
